The experimenter drove the participants onto the Smart Roads Highway and escorted them to the test area, which was on the shoulder of the Smart Roads. Participants stood approximately 6 feet apart while standing on the shoulder of the Smart Roads (see Figure 37). Participants observed a series of objects also located on the shoulder of the road at various distances. Objects included five square wooden targets painted various colors, and two mannequins (see Figure 38). Participants observed the objects and answered a series of questions regarding their perceptions of how visible the targets are and how safe they would feel on a public roadway with similar lighting (see Figure 37). Once both participants finished answering the questions for the first light condition (a combination of light type and light level), the experimenter instructed them to close their eyes briefly while the lighting condition was changed. Participants could sit down during the light change. Participants were asked to close their eyes so that they do not see the light change as this could impact their answers. Once the next light condition was ready, the participants were asked to open their eyes, observe the objects, and answer the questionnaire again. Participants repeated this process for all 14 lighting 90 conditions. Once complete, participants were shown each of the light types at the same light level (0.6 cd/m2) and were asked to answer one addition questionnaire indicating which type of lighting they preferred (see Figure 36). Figure 37. Experimental setup on the shoulder of the Virginia Smart Roads. Participants were then escorted back to VTTI and released. The entire study lasted approximately 1.5 hours (~30 minutes for consenting/intake, and ~60 minutes on the Smart Roads). 5.1.6 Analysis Two separate analysis approaches were used to answer the research questions. The first analysis approach evaluated the differences between the three different light types used in the study. The second analysis approach evaluated the differences between light levels within each light type. For the first analysis, four separate LMMs were performed for each dimension: visibility, safety and comfort, preference, and discomfort glare. Inter-item reliability for perceptions of visibility, safety and comfort, and preference was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha for all questionnaire statements. Additional analyses were only conducted for Cronbach’s alpha > 0.7, indicating a high inter-item reliability in the questionnaire responses (Bernstein & Nunnally, 1994).
